This course follows a simulated study. The study starts with [genotypes](../docs/glossary.md#genotype). A genotype is the pair of DNA letters a person carries at one chosen position. The course ends with [association](../docs/glossary.md#association) results. An association is a statistical link between a DNA difference and a trait.

All data come from a computer program. They describe no real person. You do not need any programming experience.

Follow steps 0.1 to 0.8 in order. Each step has one main action. From step 0.4, run R commands in the [console](../docs/glossary.md#console) of [RStudio](../docs/glossary.md#rstudio). Compare each result with the expected result before continuing.

Keep your computer's language and decimal settings as they are.

Validation: the R commands in this module ran without errors on Windows. The software installers and the password prompt in RStudio are checked by hand.

The student notebook for this module is `notebooks/module_00_preparation.qmd`. A [notebook](../docs/glossary.md#notebook) is a file that mixes text and R commands. The folder `lessons/` holds the source files that the author edits. You do not open them.

Lesson text, figures and simulated data: [CC BY-NC-SA 4.0](../LICENSE-CONTENT.md). Code: [MIT](../LICENSE).

```{r knit_setup, include=FALSE}
start_dir <- setwd(if (file.exists("config.R")) "." else "..")
if (requireNamespace("knitr", quietly = TRUE)) knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = getwd())
setwd(start_dir)
```

## Module 0 at a glance {#module-0-overview}

**What you will do.** You will install three free programs: [R](../docs/glossary.md#r) (the language that runs our commands), RStudio (a window that makes R easier to use) and [PLINK 2](../docs/glossary.md#plink-2) (a program that analyses genotype files). You will download the course files and the course data. Then you will run a setup check that shows your computer is ready.

**What you will learn.**

- How to find out which system and processor your computer has.
- How to install R, RStudio and PLINK 2.
- How to open a project and run a command in the console.
- Why checksums and a setup check protect your work.
- The routine you will use in every step: read, run, compare.

**How long it takes.** About 90 minutes. Package installation at 0.5 and the large data download at 0.7 take the longest.

## 0.1 Install R {#step-0-1}

<!-- step_meta: {"actions": [{"label": "Download R for Windows", "url": "https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/", "kind": "page", "os": "windows"}, {"label": "Download R for macOS", "url": "https://cran.r-project.org/bin/macosx/", "kind": "page", "os": "macos"}, {"label": "R for Linux", "url": "https://cran.r-project.org/bin/linux/", "kind": "page", "os": "linux"}], "success_line": "The R application opens.", "student_summary": "We install R, the program that runs the course commands. We choose the version that matches the computer's system and processor.", "student_kind": "outside_r", "student_action": "Check your system and processor in the computer's settings. Open [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/), choose your system and follow its installation instructions. On macOS, choose arm64 for Apple Silicon or x86_64 for Intel. Open R and check that its window appears."} -->

### What we do

Find your system and processor, then install R.

You can see this without R. On Windows, open Settings, then System, then About, and read "System type". On a Mac, click the Apple menu, then About This Mac. A line "Chip" with a name such as Apple M1 means Apple Silicon. A line "Processor" means an Intel Mac. On Linux, open Settings and look for About or System information. Menu names depend on your distribution.

Install R from [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/), the official website for R. Follow these actions:

1. Open the CRAN page. Click the link for your system: "Download R for Windows", "Download R for macOS" or "Download R for Linux".
2. On Windows, click "base" (or "install R for the first time"). Then click the link at the top that starts with "Download R" and ends with "for Windows".
3. On macOS, click the `.pkg` file for your processor. Use the `arm64` file for Apple Silicon. Use the `x86_64` file for an Intel Mac. File names on the page can change a little.
4. On Linux, follow the CRAN instructions for your distribution. Installing packages may need an administrator.
5. Open the downloaded file. Accept the default choices. Click "Next" on Windows or "Continue" on macOS until the installer ends. If the computer asks for permission or a password, give it.

After the installation you should see a new program called R. On Windows it is in the Start menu. On macOS it is in the Applications folder.

<!-- screenshot: {"kind": "screenshot", "asset_path": "Figures/screenshots/s0-1_r_download_windows.png", "platform": "windows", "placement": "what_we_do", "alt_text": "CRAN page showing the Windows R download link."} -->
<!-- screenshot: {"kind": "screenshot", "asset_path": "Figures/screenshots/s0-1_r_download_macos.png", "platform": "macos", "placement": "what_we_do", "alt_text": "CRAN page showing the Apple Silicon and Intel R installer choices."} -->

### Why

R reads the commands in the notebooks and runs them. An [R package](../docs/glossary.md#r-package) is an add-on that gives R more functions. Packages do not replace R itself.

### You need

A Windows, macOS or Linux computer. You need an internet connection to download the software and the approved data. You also need a folder where you can save files. The local data test does not need a network download. Keep free space for three things: the [encrypted archive](../docs/glossary.md#encrypted-archive) (a locked data file that needs a password), an extracted copy of it, and your results. The space you need grows as you work.

On a Mac with Apple Silicon, use the ARM64 build. On an Intel Mac, use the Intel build.

### Command

No code to run. Open R from the Start menu or the Applications folder. Check that its window opens. Step 0.4 checks the installed version after you open the course project.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

The R application opens. Its window shows version information and a `>` prompt. Your version may differ from the Windows validation environment, which used R 4.5.2. The author also tested Ubuntu extraction with R 4.6.1.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

If you cannot find the system information, ask the instructor or your institution's support team. You do not need R for this step.

If your computer blocks the installation, ask the instructor or your institution's support team for an approved installation. Do not change your system language.

</details>

### Quick check

Does the R installer also install RStudio?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>No. Install RStudio separately at step 0.3.</details>

### Files created

The R installer creates software files outside this course project.

## 0.2 Install RStudio {#step-0-2}

<!-- step_meta: {"actions": [{"label": "Download RStudio Desktop", "url": "https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/download.html", "kind": "page"}], "success_line": "RStudio opens and the Console pane shows a `>` prompt.", "student_summary": "We install RStudio, a program that makes R easier to use. We find the Console area where we will run commands.", "student_kind": "outside_r", "student_action": "Download RStudio Desktop for your system from the [official Posit page](https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/download.html) and follow its installation instructions. ### What we do

Install [RStudio Desktop](https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/download.html) and open it. R must already be installed (step 0.1). Follow these actions:

1. Open the download page. Go to "RStudio Desktop". Click the installer link for your operating system. Save the file.
2. Open the installer. On Windows, accept the default choices and click "Next" until it ends. On macOS, drag the RStudio icon onto the Applications folder icon in the window that opens. On Linux, follow the instructions on the page.
3. Start RStudio from the Start menu or the Applications folder.

You should see a window with several panes (areas). One pane is called "Console". It shows a `>` prompt.

### Why

The console runs one command at a time. The editor keeps commands in a notebook, so you can read and rerun them later. R holds values, such as loaded data, in memory. These values disappear when R restarts. Files saved on disk remain.

### You need

A working R installation from step 0.1 and the RStudio installer.

### Command

No code to run. Open RStudio from your applications menu. Find the Console pane and check that it shows a `>` prompt. You will run your first course commands at step 0.4.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

RStudio opens and the Console pane shows a `>` prompt. No calculation is required yet.

<!-- screenshot: {"kind": "screenshot", "asset_path": "Figures/screenshots/s0-2_rstudio_console_windows.png", "platform": "windows", "placement": "expected_result", "alt_text": "RStudio on Windows with the Console tab selected and an empty R prompt."} -->
<!-- screenshot: {"kind": "screenshot", "asset_path": "Figures/screenshots/s0-2_rstudio_console_macos.png", "platform": "macos", "placement": "expected_result", "alt_text": "RStudio on macOS with the Console tab selected and an empty R prompt."} -->

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

If RStudio cannot find R, check that you installed R for the correct processor. Restart RStudio after you install R. If the prompt shows `+` instead of `>`, press Escape to return to an empty prompt.

</details>

### Quick check

After restarting R, should you expect an unsaved object to remain in memory?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>No. Reload it from a saved file or rerun the command that creates it.</details>

### Files created

RStudio software files. No course data are created.

## 0.3 Download and extract the project {#step-0-3}

<!-- step_meta: {"actions": [{"label": "Download the project ZIP", "url": "https://github.com/mgentiluomo/GWAS_training_session/releases/download/project-2026.4/GWAS_course-2026.4.zip", "kind": "download"}], "success_line": "The project folder contains `config.R`, `GWAS_course.Rproj`, `R`, `lessons`, `notebooks` and `scripts`.", "student_summary": "We download and extract the complete course project. Keeping its files together lets the commands find the files they need.", "student_kind": "outside_r", "student_action": "Download [GWAS_course-2026.4.zip](https://github.com/mgentiluomo/GWAS_training_session/releases/download/project-2026.4/GWAS_course-2026.4.zip). Extract it under C:/ on Windows or your home folder on macOS or Linux, using your system's extraction tool. Open the supplied GWAS_course folder and check that it contains config.R, GWAS_course.Rproj, R, lessons, notebooks and scripts."} -->

### What we do

Download and extract the whole source project. Follow these actions:

1. Download [GWAS_course-2026.4.zip](https://github.com/mgentiluomo/GWAS_training_session/releases/download/project-2026.4/GWAS_course-2026.4.zip) from release `project-2026.4`. This fixed version contains the course project, not the encrypted data.
2. On Windows, right-click the ZIP and choose "Extract All", then "Extract". On macOS, double-click the ZIP. On Linux, use your file manager to extract it.
3. Extract it under `C:/` on Windows or your home folder on macOS and Linux. The ZIP supplies its own `GWAS_course` folder. The standard paths are `C:/GWAS_course` and `~/GWAS_course`.
4. Open that folder. You should see `config.R`, `GWAS_course.Rproj` and the folders `R`, `lessons`, `notebooks` and `scripts`.

Keep the whole folder together. You may use another writable location or folder name. Do not nest a second copy of the project inside it.

If you already use Git, a plain `git clone https://github.com/mgentiluomo/GWAS_training_session.git` also works. Its default branch is `course/2026-guided-training`. The default folder name `GWAS_training_session` is valid. Open `GWAS_course.Rproj` inside it; no folder or branch rename is needed.

### Why

The source project contains code and text. The encrypted data are separate and are downloaded at step 0.7. One project folder keeps the relative paths consistent.

Each page of this website says which project version it needs. To see your version, start R in the project folder and run `source("R/guided.R"); cfg <- guided_init()`. It prints "Project version" and the number. An older project prints no version. If a page needs a newer version than yours, download the project again from this step into a new folder.

### You need

R and RStudio from steps 0.1 and 0.2, an internet connection and a folder where you can save files.

### Command

No R code to run. Download and extract the whole project as described above.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

The project folder contains `config.R`, `GWAS_course.Rproj`, `R`, `lessons`, `notebooks` and `scripts`. The standard folder is `C:/GWAS_course` on Windows or `~/GWAS_course` on macOS and Linux. Other writable folder names also work.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

If `config.R` is missing, check that you opened the extracted project folder. Do not use a single downloaded notebook. Do not create an empty replacement file or rename a downloaded HTML page to `.R`.

</details>

### Quick check

Does downloading the source project also download the encrypted classroom data?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>No. Download the matching data at step 0.7.</details>

### Files created

The complete extracted source project.

## 0.4 Open the project and check R {#step-0-4}

<!-- step_meta: {"actions": [], "where": {"s0-4_project": "console"}, "success_line": "[1] 5", "student_summary": "We open the course project and check that R can find its files. We display the system and R version, then try a small calculation to check that commands run.", "student_plink_options": []} -->

### What we do

Open the project, then open this notebook. Follow these actions:

1. In the folder you extracted or cloned at step 0.3, double-click `GWAS_course.Rproj`. RStudio opens with the project. You should usually see the project name `GWAS_course` at the top right.
2. In the Files pane, click the folder `notebooks`. Then click `module_00_preparation.qmd`. It opens in the editor. The file `gwas_course_complete.qmd` holds all modules in one notebook, if you prefer one file. The folder `lessons` holds the source files for the author. You do not need it.
3. Run commands in the console. Always work from the [project root](../docs/glossary.md#working-directory), which is the main folder of the project.

<!-- screenshot: {"kind": "screenshot", "asset_path": "Figures/screenshots/s0-4_project_panes_windows.png", "platform": "windows", "placement": "what_we_do", "alt_text": "Course project open in RStudio on Windows, with the lesson in Source beside Console and Files."} -->
<!-- screenshot: {"kind": "screenshot", "asset_path": "Figures/screenshots/s0-4_project_panes_macos.png", "platform": "macos", "placement": "what_we_do", "alt_text": "Course project open in RStudio on macOS, with the lesson in Source beside Console and Files."} -->

### Why

A [relative path](../docs/glossary.md#relative-path) gives the place of a file starting from the working directory. The working directory is the folder where R looks first. One project root means you never copy your personal full paths into commands.

### You need

The complete extracted or cloned 2026 project from step 0.3, not one downloaded notebook. No branch change is needed.

### Command

```{r s0-4_project}
# 1. Show the folder where R looks for files.
getwd()
# 2. Check that the required project files exist.
stopifnot(file.exists("config.R"), file.exists("R/course.R"))
# 3. Show the computer's system and processor information.
Sys.info()[c("sysname", "release", "machine")]
# 4. Show the installed R version.
R.version.string
# 5. Add two numbers to check that R runs commands.
2 + 3
```

Run these commands in the RStudio Console. The function `stopifnot` stops with an error when a required condition is false. If the file checks pass, they print nothing.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

R prints the path of your project folder. The file checks finish without an error. Your folder path will differ from the author's path.

R prints your system information, its version and the result `[1] 5` from the small calculation. The R version may differ from the validation environment.

`[1] 5`

<!-- verification_note:start -->Verification: the project, version and calculation commands passed on Windows before this reordering.<!-- verification_note:end -->

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

If `config.R` is missing, close RStudio and open the project again from the extracted source folder. Do not create an empty replacement file. Do not rename a downloaded HTML page to `.R`.

</details>

### Quick check

Does a relative path starting `R/` refer to a folder on every computer's C drive?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>No. It refers to the R folder under the current project root.</details>

### Files created

RStudio may create local project settings in `.Rproj.user/`. Git ignores them.

## 0.5 Install the R packages {#step-0-5}

### What we do

Install the R packages used by the course. A package is an add-on that gives R more functions. Keep the project from step 0.4 open.

### Why

The course needs `archive`, `digest`, `getPass`, `knitr` and `rmarkdown`. Installing them now prepares the masked password prompt and the data checks.

### You need

A working project from step 0.4 and an internet connection.

### Command

```{r s0-5_packages, eval=FALSE}
# 1. Load the helper that prepares the course packages.
source("R/package_setup.R")
# 2. Install any required packages that are missing.
install_course_packages()
# 3. Load the course functions into R.
source("R/course.R")
```

The first run can take several minutes. Wait until the `>` prompt returns. Run this installation command yourself; the whole-path script omits it.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

The `>` prompt returns. If packages were installed, R also prints `Course packages are ready.` Already installed packages need no download.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check your internet connection. On Linux, the helper chooses matching ready-made Posit packages where they exist. If source installation is needed, it explains which development libraries you need. Ask the instructor or your institution's support team for help.

</details>

### Quick check

Do these R packages replace the PLINK executable?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>No. Put PLINK 2 in `bin/` at step 0.6.</details>

## 0.6 Put PLINK 2 in bin/ {#step-0-6}

<!-- step_meta: {"actions": [], "required_commands": ["s0-6_plink"], "where": {"s0-6_plink": "console"}, "success_line": "PLINK 2 2.0.0-b.1.4 is ready in bin/", "student_summary": "We prepare PLINK 2, the program that analyses the DNA data. The project already contains it, so R copies the right version for your computer into the bin folder and checks it.", "student_plink_options": []} -->

### What we do

The project package already contains PLINK 2 Beta 1.4 for Windows, macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel) and Linux. A build is a version of the program made for one system and processor. R finds your system, copies the matching build into the `bin/` folder and checks that it is the right file. You do not download anything. Follow these actions:

1. Keep the project from step 0.4 open in RStudio.
2. Run the command below in the console.
3. Read the last line it prints. It should say that PLINK 2 is ready in `bin/`.

Run only the command of this step. Do not open the programs inside `third_party/` by hand. On macOS, the system can block such a file and move it to the Bin. The command copies a clean build into `bin/`, and that copy is not blocked.

The program is `plink2.exe` on Windows and `plink2` on macOS or Linux. This file is the [executable](../docs/glossary.md#executable), the file your computer can run. The builds are in `third_party/plink2/programs/`. R never changes a different PLINK 2 file that you put in `bin/` yourself. It tells you instead. If you cloned the project with Git, the builds are not in the clone. R then downloads the pinned build and checks it in the same way.

You can still get PLINK 2 from the official page, <https://www.cog-genomics.org/plink/2.0/>. Use it only if R cannot prepare the program, or if your lecturer asks for a different version. Choose the build whose name matches your system and processor from step 0.1. Extract the ZIP file and copy only `plink2.exe` (or `plink2`) into `bin/`. If you are not sure that your processor supports AVX2 (an instruction set of the processor), choose the 64-bit build without AVX2.

### Why

PLINK 2 reads the genotype file formats. It computes [quality control](../docs/glossary.md#quality-control) (QC) and association statistics. QC means checks that find samples or data that cannot be trusted. PLINK 1.9 is a different program, so it does not replace PLINK 2. The course checks the file against a stored SHA-256 value, a fingerprint of the file. This shows that you have the exact program that the course was tested with. The tested version is stored in one place, the settings file `config.R`. The setup check at step 0.8 reports your version and warns you if it differs.

### You need

The extracted project from step 0.3 and the R session from step 0.5. Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit Intel or AMD), macOS, or Linux x86_64 with glibc 2.31 or newer. For Windows ARM or Linux ARM, ask support for a compatible version.

### Command

```{r s0-6_plink, eval=FALSE}
# 1. Load the helper that prepares PLINK 2.
source("R/plink_setup.R")
# 2. Copy the PLINK 2 build for your computer into the bin folder and check it.
prepare_course_plink()
```

Run this command yourself; the whole-path script omits it. It finishes in a few seconds.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

R prints one line. On the first run it is `PLINK 2 2.0.0-b.1.4 is ready in bin/ (windows-x86_64, from the package).` The system name in brackets matches your computer. If the file is already there, R prints `The course PLINK 2 program is already in bin/ and has the expected version.` The folder `bin` now holds `plink2.exe` on Windows, or `plink2` on macOS or Linux.

<!-- screenshot: {"kind": "screenshot", "asset_path": "Figures/screenshots/s0-6_plink_executable_windows.png", "platform": "windows", "placement": "expected_result", "alt_text": "Windows File Explorer showing plink2.exe in the course bin folder."} -->
<!-- screenshot: {"kind": "screenshot", "asset_path": "Figures/screenshots/s0-6_plink_executable_macos.png", "platform": "macos", "placement": "expected_result", "alt_text": "macOS Finder showing plink2 in the course bin folder."} -->

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

If R says that your computer cannot use the programs of the course, download PLINK 2 yourself from the official page, as described above. For Windows ARM or Linux ARM, ask support.

On macOS, run only the command of this step, `prepare_course_plink()`. Do not open the programs inside `third_party/` by hand. A browser marks the ZIP file as coming from the internet, and macOS copies this mark to every file inside it. macOS can then block a program that you start yourself and move it to the Bin. The copy in `bin/` does not carry the mark.

If macOS shows a warning about `bin/plink2`, choose "Done". Do not choose "Move to Bin". Then open the Terminal in the project folder and type `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine bin/plink2`. This command removes the quarantine mark, the mark that macOS adds to files from the internet. Then run the command of step 0.6 again.

If `bin/plink2` has disappeared, run the command of step 0.6 again. If the program in `third_party/` has disappeared too, extract the project ZIP again and run the command once more.

You can also open System Settings, then Privacy & Security, find the message for `plink2` and click "Open Anyway". Follow [Apple's instructions](https://support.apple.com/en-us/102445).

On Linux, PLINK 2 needs glibc 2.31 or newer. If you see the message "Kernel too old" or a glibc error, your system is too old for this build. Ask support. If the file lacks permission to run, type `chmod u+x bin/plink2` in the project folder.

On Windows, SmartScreen may show "Windows protected your PC". Review "More info" and use "Run anyway" if your institution permits it. If that option is unavailable, ask support. See [Microsoft's SmartScreen guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/package-and-deploy/smartscreen-reputation).

If R says that a SHA-256 value does not match, do not use the file. Download the project package again, or ask the instructor.

</details>

### Quick check

Does the command at step 0.6 download PLINK 2 from the internet?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>No. It copies the build that is already in the project package. Only if the package has no build for your system does it download the pinned build, and it checks the SHA-256 value first.</details>

### Files created

`bin/plink2.exe` or `bin/plink2`. It stays outside [Git](../docs/glossary.md#git), the tool that records versions of the project files.

## 0.7 Request the password and download the data {#step-0-7}

<!-- step_meta: {"actions": [{"label": "Request the course password", "url": "https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/data-access", "kind": "page"}, {"label": "Course data release", "url": "https://github.com/mgentiluomo/GWAS_training_session/releases/tag/data-2026.1", "kind": "page"}], "required_commands": ["s0-7_data"], "where": {"s0-7_data": "console"}, "success_line": "Course data are ready: 108 files verified.", "student_summary": "University of Pisa users request the password through the [data access form](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/data-access) with an email address at unipi.it or one of its subdomains. Other users write to [manuel.gentiluomo@unipi.it](mailto:manuel.gentiluomo@unipi.it). We then download and check the course data, entering the password only in the prompt that hides the letters, never in a file.", "student_plink_options": []} -->

### What we do

Request the course password, then download the matching encrypted data with `download_course_data()`. The data are published in [GitHub Release data-2026.1](https://github.com/mgentiluomo/GWAS_training_session/releases/tag/data-2026.1). The download URLs and SHA-256 checksums are set in `config.R`. The package contains 108 files.

### Why

The source project contains code and text. The encrypted package contains the data. A [checksum](../docs/glossary.md#checksum) is a short code calculated from a file. If the file changes, the code changes. Checksums detect changed or damaged downloads. The password decrypts the archive. A correct password does not replace the checksum check.

### You need

The complete project folder, R and an internet connection. The command below downloads `course-data-2026.1.zip` and its small manifest file, `MANIFEST.tsv`, for you.

Request the password with your university email through the [data access form](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/data-access). In class, you can scan the QR code to open the same form. The form accepts University of Pisa email addresses at `unipi.it` and all its subdomains. Examples include `studenti.unipi.it`, `phd.unipi.it` and `biologia.unipi.it`. It sends the password automatically to these addresses. Other users should write to [manuel.gentiluomo@unipi.it](mailto:manuel.gentiluomo@unipi.it). The password changes every academic year. Do not share it. It never appears in the repository or on the site.

The packages from step 0.5 and the executable from step 0.6. Keep the project from step 0.4 open.

### Command

Run this command in the RStudio console. It does not run automatically when the
notebook is rendered:

```{r s0-7_data, eval=FALSE}
# 1. Download the course data and check that the files are complete and unchanged.
download_course_data()
```

The function uses `getPass` to ask for a masked password. Type it and press
Enter. You will not see the letters appear. Do not write the password in this
notebook, a shared script or your command history. You do not need 7-Zip.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

On the first successful run, R prints `Course data are ready: 108 files verified.` On a later run with verified data, it prints `Course data are already ready: 108 files verified. Nothing to do.` It does not download or ask for the password again. The data are in the folder `data/course/`. The archive and its small manifest file (a list of the files inside) must both match their configured SHA-256 values. R also checks every extracted data file.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

If the download fails, check your internet connection. As a local fallback,
open the release page linked above. Save `course-data-2026.1.zip` and
`MANIFEST.tsv` together in one folder. Then run:

```r
download_course_data(zip_path = file.choose())
```

A file selection window opens. Choose the published ZIP file. Do not choose
the manifest or the project ZIP. The helper checks the same SHA-256 values.

If the data folder exists but cannot be verified, R reports what it found.
This includes a missing manifest, missing files or changed files. For the
standard folder, run the exact recovery command:

```r
download_course_data(overwrite = TRUE)
```

The helper verifies a fresh copy first. It then moves the old folder and its
manifest to a dated backup before replacing them. It prints the backup path.
It never silently deletes the old data. Use that backup if you need earlier work.

Older installations did not keep the verification manifest. They need this
backup and reinstall once. Later runs verify the saved manifest and all data
files without a download or a password prompt.

If R says that the release is not configured, download the current course
project again. If the password is wrong, check your typing and contact the
instructor if needed. Never bypass a checksum failure. See
[troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

If the checksum differs but the password is accepted, should you use that download?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>No. Obtain the approved matching package before continuing.</details>

### Files created

Verified data in `data/course/` and the verification manifest at
`data/course.MANIFEST.tsv`. The manifest stays beside the folder, so the
package still contains 108 files. R removes temporary download and extraction
files. Data, manifests and passwords are never added to Git.

## 0.8 Run the setup check {#step-0-8}

<!-- step_meta: {"actions": [], "where": {"s0-8_preflight": "console"}, "success_line": "Preflight passed.", "student_summary": "We run the setup check to test the R packages, data files and PLINK 2. PLINK reads 20 DNA positions and writes a report, including a test in a folder whose name contains spaces and non-English letters.", "student_plink_options": [{"label": "test reading data and writing a report", "options": [{"name": "--bfile", "explanation": "Reads the BED, BIM and FAM input files named sim2026_lab in data/course/lab_export/."}, {"name": "--autosome", "explanation": "Keeps only DNA positions on chromosomes 1 to 22."}, {"name": "--thin-count", "explanation": "Selects 20 DNA positions at random for this small test."}, {"name": "--seed", "explanation": "Uses 20261111 as the starting number for the random selection so it can be repeated."}, {"name": "--freq", "explanation": "Writes a report showing how common each version of a DNA letter is at the selected positions."}, {"name": "--out", "explanation": "Starts the report file names with results/guided/s0-8_probe in the standard project layout; the helper also tests a folder name with spaces and non-English letters."}]}]} -->

### What we do

Run the setup check. It tests the R packages, the [locale](../docs/glossary.md#locale) (your computer's language and number settings), the integrity of the genotype files, and a small PLINK read and write operation. This test uses 20 [variants](../docs/glossary.md#variant), which are DNA positions that differ between people. At the end you should see the message `Preflight passed.`

### Why

A program can print its version and still fail to read data. It can also fail to write results in a folder path that has spaces or non-English letters. A test with a real operation finds these failures before a long analysis.

### You need

The executable from step 0.6 and the verified data from step 0.7. The standard guided data folder is `data/course/`. Some people use an existing external installation. For them, the environment variable `COURSE_DATA_DIR` can name the extracted data, and `COURSE_OUTPUT_DIR` can name a separate output folder. These optional variables contain paths and never passwords.

### Command

```{r s0-8_preflight}
# 1. Create a separate place in R to hold the course settings.
settings <- new.env(parent = baseenv())
# 2. Read the course settings from config.R.
sys.source("config.R", settings)
# 3. Show the PLINK version used to test the course.
settings$course_settings$tested_plink_version
# 4. Run the setup checks, including the small PLINK test.
source("scripts/preflight.R")
```

Terminal equivalent: `Rscript --vanilla scripts/preflight.R`. The option `--vanilla` starts R without saved workspaces and startup files. Inside the setup check, the R helper runs PLINK with these options. The exact command, with your paths and resource settings, is printed and recorded.

- `--bfile` selects the input files by their shared name prefix. The prefix covers files in the [BED/BIM/FAM](../docs/glossary.md#bed-bim-fam) format.

- `--autosome` keeps only autosomal variants, which are those on chromosomes 1 to 22.

- `--thin-count 20` keeps a small subset of 20 variants, chosen at random.

- `--seed 20261111` sets the starting number of the random choice, so the sampling is repeatable.

- `--freq` reports allele frequencies, which show how common each allele is.

- `--out` sets the prefix of the output files.

For the standard project layout, the plain PLINK command is:

```sh
bin/plink2 --bfile data/course/lab_export/sim2026_lab --autosome --thin-count 20 --seed 20261111 --freq --out results/guided/s0-8_probe --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

`--threads 2` limits PLINK to two worker threads, which are parts of the computer that work at the same time; `--memory 2048` sets the main workspace of PLINK to 2048 MiB (about 2 gigabytes). On Windows, the executable is `bin\plink2.exe`. The helper also runs a second test on purpose, with a folder name that has non-English letters. It translates that path in a safe way.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

The setup check prints one short line per check, with `PASS` or the problem. It keeps the full PLINK output in `results/guided/preflight.txt` (or the folder selected by `COURSE_OUTPUT_DIR`). The tested PLINK version is printed before the checks.

`Preflight passed.`

The guided starting data have 2,016 sample wells and 299,523 variants, representing 2,000 simulated people. PLINK finishes the frequency test on 20 variants. The report can show sex as "ambiguous". This is normal at this stage: the starting FAM has no recorded sex. The probe reads autosomal variants and does not perform the sex check from step 3.3. A path such as `PATHCH~1` in the report is the safe form of a folder with non-English letters.

<!-- verification_note:start -->Verification: the same package, genotype and PLINK read/write checks passed on Windows before this output change.<!-- verification_note:end -->

<!-- screenshot: {"kind": "screenshot", "asset_path": "Figures/screenshots/s0-8_preflight_success_windows.png", "platform": "windows", "placement": "expected_result", "alt_text": "Successful Windows setup check in RStudio, with Preflight passed and the R prompt visible."} -->
<!-- screenshot: {"kind": "screenshot", "asset_path": "Figures/screenshots/s0-8_preflight_success_macos.png", "platform": "macos", "placement": "expected_result", "alt_text": "Successful macOS setup check in RStudio, with Preflight passed and the R prompt visible."} -->

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Do not run later analysis steps until the setup check succeeds. The setup check explains which package is unavailable or whether the PLINK program is missing. On Windows, the script clears locale requests that R cannot use. This change lasts for the current session only, and your Windows language stays unchanged. Startup warnings can appear before the script has a chance to run. On Linux, the package preparation chooses matching ready-made Posit packages where they exist. If a package must be built from source code, the script explains which development libraries you need. If the course data are missing (step 0.7 is not done), the setup check prints a warning, skips the data check and ends with `Preflight passed with a warning: course data are missing.` Finish step 0.7 and run it again.

</details>

### Quick check

Why does the setup check write a frequency report rather than only print a version?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>It tests actual data reading and file writing, including a path containing spaces and non-English characters.</details>

### Files created

`results/guided/software_versions.txt`, `results/guided/preflight.txt` and PLINK test reports in its `path check/` folder. If `COURSE_OUTPUT_DIR` is set, the same files go there instead. No source input is changed.

## Module 0 recap {#module-0-recap}

- You found your operating system and processor, and installed R, RStudio and PLINK 2.
- You downloaded the course project and the encrypted data, and checked them with SHA-256 checksums.
- The archive reported `Course data are ready: 108 files verified.`
- The setup check ran PLINK on 20 variants and printed `Preflight passed.`
- The starting data have 2,016 sample wells and 299,523 variants, which represent 2,000 simulated people.
- You learned the routine for every step: read, run, compare.

### How to use this guide {#using-this-guide}

Use the same routine at every step: read, run, compare. Follow these actions:

1. Read "What we do", "Why" and "You need".
2. Run the command in the console.
3. Open "Show the expected result" and compare it with your result.
4. If your result differs, open "If something goes wrong".
5. Answer the quick check.

A successful check at step 0.8. Keep the output files and the notebook together in their documented places. The [glossary](../docs/glossary.md) explains the terms used in the course, including quality control, alleles and association.

Every file that the steps create is saved in the folder `results/guided/` of the project. The list "Files created" at the end of each step gives the file names. To look at a file in RStudio, open the Files pane, click `results`, then `guided`.

Read the list of checkpoints that came with your package. This command changes no files:

```{r course_progress}
source("R/guided.R")
cfg <- guided_init()
where_am_i(data_dir = cfg$data_dir, work_dir = cfg$out)
```

Terminal equivalent: call the R helper through Rscript after you set the same project paths. There is no PLINK command that reports course progress. A [checkpoint](../docs/glossary.md#checkpoint) is a saved state of the course files at the end of a step. The helper `check_step("3.2")` compares step 3.2 with a supplied checkpoint. The helper `restore_checkpoint("3.2")` rebuilds the state after step 3.1, so that you can restart step 3.2. Both protect existing output folders.

Before you start the analysis, every state in the updated checkpoint index is `not verified`. Full genotype sets exist at 2.8, 3.8, 4.6 and 5.7. The other states are rebuilt from stored lists and transformations. Diagnostic and analysis files have their own small checkpoints. The list has about 30 rows, one for each saved state.

A missing checkpoint does not mean that you failed the analysis. The course package may not supply the baseline, lists or index that the checkpoint needs. Ask for the matching updated package. Do not mix versions. A copied list alone does not recreate the genotypes.

To restart step 4.2, which completed step's files do you need?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>Step 4.1, from the same course data version.</details>
